slides.lead: Your toddler is not being silly. They are taking notes.
slides.sub: Children trained to spot pointless actions copied them anyway. A puzzle box, 63 children, and 147 times the odds of copying.

figure.label: higher odds of copying a useless step after watching an adult do it

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
Yale researchers trained 63 three- to five-year-olds to spot an adult's pointless actions, and praised them for it.

Then they showed each child how to open a clear plastic puzzle box, adding two steps that visibly did nothing.

slides.head: What the children did

stat.label: higher odds of using the useless mechanism than children who had never watched an adult at all

slides.body: Warning them did not work. A separate group was told outright to skip anything silly, reminded seconds before their turn, and copied it anyway.

slides.head: The one thing that stopped it
slides.body:
Splitting the box into two halves that no longer touched. Once the extra action could not physically matter, the copying vanished.

So this is not blind mimicry. It is a three-year-old building a theory of how the object works, and treating your hands as the best evidence available.

slides.head: The catch, and the point
slides.body:
One lab, one task, 63 children. Since then the finding has replicated across cultures, varying in how much children copy rather than whether.

Worth remembering the next time you jiggle a key in a lock, or tap the side of the toaster. Someone is taking notes.
